stemBlocks.value: The distance d needed to stop a car varies directly as the square of its speed s. A car travelling at 70 km/h requires a stopping distance of 40 m. Find the stopping distance when the speed is 80 km/h.
Think first: The distance depends on the square of the speed, so the speeds must be squared before you compare them.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p114-q02 from workbook page 114.

solutionSteps.instruction: Write the variation statement as an equation.
Substitute d = 40 and s = 70 to find k.
Round sensibly for a practical distance.

strategyBlocks.value: Write d = ks², use d = 40 when s = 70 to find k, then substitute s = 80.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: The stopping distance is 12800/245 m ≈ 52.2 m

whyThisWorks.value: Because d is proportional to s², multiplying the speed by a factor multiplies the stopping distance by the square of that factor. Here the speed rises by a factor of 80/70, so the distance rises by (80/70)² ≈ 1.31 — a 14% increase in speed causes roughly a 31% increase in stopping distance. That squared relationship is the reason small increases in speed matter so much on the road.

commonErrors.misconception: Using d = ks and scaling the distance by 80/70 instead of (80/70)².
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Using d = ks and scaling the distance by 80/70 instead of (80/70)².

commonErrors.misconception: Squaring only after dividing, e.g. computing 40 × 80²/70 rather than 40 × (80/70)².
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Squaring only after dividing, e.g. computing 40 × 80²/70 rather than 40 × (80/70)².

commonErrors.misconception: Rounding k too early and losing accuracy in the final answer.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Rounding k too early and losing accuracy in the final answer.

examTip.value: For a square-law variation you can skip finding k: use d₂ = d₁ × (s₂/s₁)², which is faster and avoids rounding errors.
